(3) The Lawyer's Role. Mrs. Williams was represented 
by the Legal 
Assistance Office of the bar association. That office "was willing to concede 
that the store could repossess the stereo record player for nonpayment, but 
what stirred them to action was that the seller sought to scoop up all that it 
had ever smd to Ora." Skilton & Helstad, fn. h, p. 684, above. As a legal 
precedent, the court's ruling on unconscionability is more significant for 
consumers generally than any victory Mrs. Williams could have won on the 
basis of interpretation 
of her contract. Legal-aid lawyers report that they can 
often settle complaints of individual consumer debtors on favorable terms. 
In such a situ: tion, what is the duty of the lawyer? Should they urge such a 
client to forgo settlement on a narrow claim in the hope of obtaining a 
landmark ruling on a broader principle like unconscionability? What are the 
ethical considerations? 
(4) The Question of Remedies. In Frostifresh Corp. v. Reynoso the seller 
of a freezer sued the Reynosos for the unpaid balance of the price. The 
Reynosos had made only one payment of $32 on a purchase price of $348. 
The trial comt made a simple deduction, and gave judgment for $316. On 
appeal, the Judgment was reversed, and the trial court was directed to give 
judgment for the "net cost for the refrigerator-freezer, 
plus a reasonable 
profit, in addition to trucking and service charges necessarily incurred and 
reasonable finance charges." Here are two comments on the Frostifresh case: 
"This case means that sellers can charge the most exorbitant rates, 
secure in the knowledge that at the worst they will be able to recover a 
reasonable profit plus all their expenses." Ray Narral, Interview, in The Law 
and the Low Income Consumer 330 (Carol H. Katz ed., 1968). 
"It must be recognized that even in the poverty situations, putting aside 
the cases of fraud and high pressure in home sales, the buyers do want the 
goods. Even in the famous Frostifresh case, the question of remedies was 
complicated by the fact that the Spanish-speaking people deceived into 
buying a home freezer at a high price chose to keep the freezer. Thus we 
cannot adopt restrictions on remedies so punitive as to put the credit sellers 
in the poverty areas, and their financers, out of business. Despite the present 
high social cost, they serve a social purpose." Homer Kripke, Consumer 
Credit Regulation: A Creditor-Oriented Viewpoint, 68 Colum. L. Rev. 455, 
478 (1968). 
For an alternative method
